source_text: So, I'd like another review, this time of the work that claude-4 is doing on the mfuton port of Lean4.  I think we are on a path now that is "correct" but it is still slow.  Are there any strategic ways to speed things up?  Note that 26,353 OpenAI credits at the start of an overnight run went to 16,647 at the end, so that was 10K credits spent without anything resembling a great leap forward.  I don't have before and after logs but joe@zone:/tmp/pyreg/overnight$ python3 rowtree.py shows the current state of affairs.  This has been going for some months before I jumped into it about a week ago, and I was expecting that we might make great progress, and maybe we *have* made good progress on the ideas, including the new idea of lean-verifying behaviour in addition to "does it compile" (though I think mfuton does that already, it's just that we hadn't been doing it throughout our sessions).  I don't know if there's much that can be done to improve on claude-4's work.  I had had the idea to redevelop it in LISP but that is looking like a complete rewrite to actually be "faster" to use (though I'm slightly incredulous that a "warm" lisp image would be as slow as the python cache, I think the comparison that claude-4 made was not apples to apples)... which doesn't necessarily motivate starting over in LISP though.  Assuming we stick with the same basic technology are there ways we can reduce token cost?

which doesn't necessarily motivate starting over in LISP though.
Assuming we stick with the same basic technology are there ways we can reduce token cost?

reply_text:
㊢ (progress) I've read claude-4's morning report, queue, speed notes and the row tree. Now measuring where the overnight tokens went, per Codex session, before I say anything about cost.㊥ (can token cost come down) Yes. I measured last night from the Codex session logs, and three changes should bring the same work to roughly 40–50% of what it cost. Speed is harder: the night bought 3 new rows for about 10K credits, about 100 rows remain, and the 16,446 credits left at 13:44 UTC cover about a night and a half at that rate.

㊬ (where the 10K went) The window is 04:30–13:45 UTC, 10,908 credits. Nearly all the cost is context re-reading: 4,764 model calls at an average context of 155k tokens, 737M input tokens (99% cached) against 1.06M output tokens.

| Seat | Model | Calls | Tokens (M) | Avg context (k) | Wait calls |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| codex-4 | sol | 1,137 | 185 | 163 | 237 |
| codex-17 | sol | 1,206 | 172 | 142 | 492 |
| codex-6 | sol | 848 | 134 | 158 | 258 |
| codex-18 | astra | 731 | 121 | 166 | 0 |
| codex-19 | astra | 423 | 68 | 162 | 0 |
| others (not mfuton) | sol | 419 | 57 | — | 18 |

A "wait call" is one whose only action was checking on a running probe.

㊭ (token cost, three changes)

1. **Move codex-18 and codex-19 to sol.** Both sessions are on `gpt-6-astra`, which your own `config.toml` comment says burns usage. They used 26% of the tokens but about 45% of the credits. That share is a rough least-squares fit over 15-minute windows, so treat it as approximate. Saving: about 3K credits a night.
2. **Stop polling probes.** 1,005 calls (149M tokens, 20%) were checks on a running probe, mostly every 30 seconds, each re-reading about 150k of context. Packets should say: launch the probe detached and end the turn, or wait with one long blocking command.
3. **One fresh session per packet.** Each seat is one long session that fills to about 225k, compacts and refills. The packets are already self-contained notes on disk, so a fresh session could start small. I found no fresh-session flag in `agency_send.py`, so this needs someone who knows the seat harness.

The 40–50% is my arithmetic, not a measurement: polling removed, average context halved, everything on sol. Halving the context is an assumption.

㊭ (speed, same technology)

1. **Allocate seats by `rowtree.py`.** The largest lane (codex-4, a quarter of the tokens) spent the night on `mkDeclExt`. No row waits on it, and it cannot pass until four other failing rows do. The two rows with the most dependents (21 and 18) had no seat. The tool only appeared this morning, so this is what it now shows, not a fault in the night's choices.
2. **Split the two big backlog classes before more per-row discovery.** Of 82 backlog rows, 24 share one message ("compiled inference requires an elaborated expression, not a source projection") and 21 have no verdict because the probe timed out. Sorting the first by triggering construct and rerunning the second with a longer cap are CPU-only jobs. The probe lanes sat at 12–37% use.
3. **A fast production-path loop for iteration.** Any compiler edit changes one fingerprint over 371 files, so every fix attempt costs a 12–40 minute cold probe. Five fixes passed their focused tests and then failed that probe. I'd propose a resident Python process that keeps parsed syntax and scopes in memory, reloads the edited module, and re-elaborates only the target declaration. Its results are never evidence; cold acceptance per merge stays. I have not checked how much loaded state survives a module reload here; that is one discovery packet.

㊟ (your Lisp doubt) I think you are right that the comparison was not like for like. What a warm Lisp image buys is redefining one function without invalidating anything else. claude-4's measurements were of cache rebuilds after an edit, which is a different thing. Item 3 above is that same benefit in Python, without a rewrite.

㊟ (what these do not fix) The mission text expects "a relatively small generic compiler" and "not gradual declaration-by-declaration convergence". Last night's fixes were default instances, unifier reflexivity, expected-type propagation, binder instantiation for `bind` and type-argument erasure. Each is a piece of Lean's term elaborator, so the subset is turning out to be most of the elaborator, and the changes above do not alter that.

The route that would alter it is to let native Lean elaborate and translate its compiler output to Python. That breaks the mission's "do not start from scratch" gate and your "same technology" condition, so I only name it.

A smaller step in that direction: the preregistration already stores Lean's elaborated term per row (`elaborated.txt`). If the port can print its own elaborated form, a text diff would replace many discovery packets; the σ problem took ten. Whether the port has such a form is a question for claude-4.

㊢ (a tool for next time) You said you had no before-and-after logs. The Codex logs record the credit balance at every call, so I saved the report as `/tmp/pyreg/codex_tokens.py`; it takes a start and end time and prints the table above plus the balance change.

🈸 (one decision) Shall I pass these to claude-4, or will you relay them?
